questions.q: According to this lesson, what actually breaks about manual DBA tasks like index maintenance or integrity checks?
options: Not any single task itself, but that it stops being sustainable once done by hand across ten, fifty, or more databases
The tasks are impossible to perform manually even once
SQL Server Agent cannot run any of these tasks under any circumstances
Manual tasks are always faster than automated ones regardless of scale
questions.explain: The lesson's point is the manual ceiling: each task is fine for one database, but doing it by hand fifty times a week is where DBAs lose time and things quietly stop getting checked.

questions.q: Which three Chapter 9-10 tasks does this lesson name as the first automation candidates?
options: Index maintenance, DBCC CHECKDB integrity checks, and backup verification
Creating logins, writing stored procedures, and designing schemas
Configuring firewalls, VNets, and private endpoints
Setting up Always On Availability Groups
questions.explain: These are the routine maintenance tasks from Chapter 9 that don't scale by hand once database counts grow.

questions.q: Why does this chapter go beyond SQL Server Agent alone, per the lesson?
options: Because Lesson 59 already established Agent has real limits in Azure SQL Database, so Azure needs a wider automation toolbox
Because SQL Server Agent doesn't exist anywhere in Azure in any form
Because CLI and PowerShell replace all T-SQL entirely
Because Elastic Jobs are only for on-premises SQL Server
questions.explain: Agent's role in Azure SQL Database is narrower than on-prem, so this chapter introduces CLI/PowerShell, IaC, and Elastic Jobs as the wider toolbox.

questions.q: What is the 'control plane,' as this lesson uses the term?
options: The Azure management layer that CLI, PowerShell, and ARM/Bicep talk to — distinct from the T-SQL layer inside a database
A synonym for the SQL Server Agent job scheduler
A physical server that hosts all Azure SQL databases
The name of the Elastic Jobs agent database
questions.explain: The control plane is the management layer for Azure resources themselves, separate from querying data inside a database.

questions.q: What is the order of this chapter's five-lesson arc, as previewed here?
options: CLI/PowerShell, then ARM/Bicep, then Elastic Jobs, then deployment automation with alerting
Elastic Jobs first, then backups, then high availability
Migration planning, then assessment, then cutover
Query tuning, then indexing, then statistics
questions.explain: The chapter moves from scripting tools, to infrastructure as code, to the Azure SQL Database job scheduler, to tying automation into a real deployment pipeline.
